# RUNTIME-02 — Constitutional Materiality Assessment

## 1. Governing test

The engine owns invocation and transition. The invoked instrument owns doctrine. Evidence objects represent state. OPERATIONS implements the transition without acquiring the invoked authority.

## 2. Phase/function assessment

| Function | A — invariant | B — when authority exists | C — substantive answer | D — implementation-specific | E — prevents execution | Constitutional disposition |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| Runtime entry and context | Yes | Yes | No | Partly | Yes | Phase boundary and mandatory inputs are constitutional; collection mechanics are operational. |
| Pre-classification | Yes | Indirectly | No | Partly | Yes | The contamination-control ordering is constitutional; classifiers and algorithms remain external. |
| Domain determination | Yes | Yes | Yes, but only in invoked owners | Yes | Yes | The invocation and distinct-return requirement are constitutional; every substantive determination remains with its domain owner. |
| Authority resolution | Yes | Yes | Yes, in Annex D/ARBITRATION where collision exists | Partly | Yes | Invocation, no-collision/arbitration branching and scoped return are constitutional. Merits and procedure remain external. |
| Response/action preparation | Yes | No | Yes, in applicable domains | Yes | Indirectly | The requirement for a bounded candidate downstream of authority is constitutional. Composition algorithms are operational/domain-specific. |
| Execution-boundary evaluation | Yes | Yes | Consumes external determinations | Partly | Yes | Constitutional in full as an admissibility transition; evaluation mechanics remain operational. |
| Bounded commitment | Yes | Yes | No | Partly | Yes | Constitutional as the last authorisation-preserving transition before execution. Snapshot and record mechanics are operational. |
| Execution | Yes | No | No | Yes | Yes | The requirement that only the committed candidate executes and that material change interrupts is constitutional. Tools and action mechanics are operational. |
| Representation and delivery | Yes | No | Yes, in Annex L/ETHICS/RELATION | Yes | Yes | Consumption of actual state and non-manufacture of success are constitutional. Rendering mechanics and substantive expression doctrine remain external. |
| Preservation/closure/reassessment | Yes | Indirectly | No | Yes | Yes | Mandatory closure, expiry and valid re-entry targets are constitutional. Schemas, retention and logging mechanics remain external. |
| Tendeka | Yes | Yes | Trigger/release doctrine remains in Article V and `AEON-001-SCH-01` | Yes | Yes | Cross-cutting engine transition; do not absorb trigger merits, propagation doctrine or procedure. |
| Referral | Yes | Yes | Competent authority decides | Yes | Yes | Constitutional transition; routing/custody mechanics are operational. |
| Agent/tool sub-action re-entry | Yes | Yes | No | Partly | Yes | A new material target, authority, permission or effect must re-enter the engine; framework hooks are operational. |

## 3. Tendeka adjudication

Tendeka is best represented in the engine as a cross-cutting constitutional control-flow primitive, but it remains independently source-authoritative under Article V and `CAM-BS2025-AEON-001-SCH-01`.

The engine therefore owns only:

- where a valid Tendeka result can interrupt phase progression;
- prohibition on advancing an affected pathway;
- permitted severable continuation;
- preservation of the paused state; and
- the phase to which processing may return after competent release, restriction or referral.

The Tendeka Schedule retains:

- trigger scope;
- mandatory pause;
- competent release authority;
- distributed propagation and severability; and
- non-derogation.

OPERATIONS retains detection procedure, custody, routing, records, logging and implementation mechanics. No Tendeka protection is deleted or weakened.

## 4. One Schedule versus multiple Schedules

| Criterion | Option A — one constitutional Runtime Processing Schedule | Option B — multiple constitutional phase Schedules |
|---|---|---|
| End-to-end state-machine legibility | Complete in one instrument | Requires cross-document reconstruction |
| Transition ownership | Singular | Distributed and drift-prone |
| Domain-authority containment | Achievable through explicit invocation/non-absorption contract | Modular documents may still absorb doctrine and duplicate transitions |
| Interrupt/re-entry integrity | One transition table can govern all phases | Requires repeated cross-Schedule contracts |
| Conformance testing | Deterministic graph and invocation checks | Multi-file graph and version coupling |
| Scope-creep risk | Real, controlled by lean phase contracts | Real in every phase Schedule, plus aggregate duplication risk |
| Current repository fit | `AEON-003-SCH-02` already owns processing order and phase transitions | Would recreate instruments just retired during decomposition |

**Decision: Option A.** Authority coherence and state-machine integrity outweigh document-size modularity. The Schedule must remain lean: state, invocation, transition and invariant only.

## 5. Placement decision

`CAM-BS2025-AEON-003-SCH-02` is the source-authoritative constitutional state machine.

`CAM-EQ2026-OPERATIONS-001-PLATINUM` implements the Schedule through subordinate procedures. `CAM-EQ2026-OPERATIONS-001-SUP-02` owns exceptional transition custody and exact return mechanics. `CAM-EQ2026-OPERATIONS-007-PLATINUM` owns applicability, conformance and proportionate evidence. None becomes the engine.

The provisional `CAM-EQ2026-OPERATIONS-009-PLATINUM` recommendation is withdrawn. No such instrument should be created.

## 6. Scope-control conclusion

The constitutional engine may name an invoked owner and the state that must be returned. It must not reproduce classifiers, scoring, arbitration merits, security taxonomy, identity doctrine, detailed verification algorithms, tool procedure, logging schema or provider-specific control logic.
